finding: Calhoun describes a pattern of frequent production pauses since 2021 and defends it as the way Boeing improves, even at investors' expense.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: She said, you want to introduce this new airplane, a derivative, yes, but a new airplane. And 9 months from now, you'll have an engineered solution to it, to this issue. And why is that the right call? And in my view, it was a sound, principled position to take.
finding: Under congressional pressure Boeing withdrew its MAX 7 time-limited exemption request, accepting certification delay until an engineered anti-ice fix exists.
trigger: Senator Duckworth objection to MAX 7 anti-ice exemption after Alaska 1282
response: Withdrew MAX 7 exemption request

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: the pause is going to be helpful for us in so many ways in the sense that, that supply chain, they're going to keep running according to that master schedule. It's good for us if some buffers get developed and some of the more stressed suppliers get ahead of the game.
finding: Calhoun framed the FAA-imposed pause as a chance to build supplier buffers, confirming that the supply chain was the governing constraint on the ramp.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: right now, we're in the position where we have to do things like pause the line. And we are doing that so that we can get the benefit of our audit, we can get the benefit of our own inspection protocols, and that will just slow the line.
finding: Boeing paused 737 final assembly to absorb audit and inspection findings, accepting lower output.
trigger: FAA 6-week audit with 26 inspectors after Alaska 1282
response: Line pauses and slower final assembly

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: our overall approach will be that we could avoid instability and broad movements in the supply chain by holding supplier build rates pretty steady. And that's important because that's what they've asked us to do.
finding: Boeing held supplier build rates steady while final assembly slowed, at suppliers' request, to avoid supply-chain whiplash.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: since November of 2022, we've been staffed at 38 per month for the 37. And what that has allowed us to do is, yes, work on shadow factory but also create an environment where we're doing more and more training of our people
finding: Boeing staffed the 737 line ahead of output at 38/month from late 2022, using the surplus for rework and training so it is ready for later rate increases.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: when you get out to our time frame of '25, '26, you have a 37 cash margin profile that gets back pretty close to what it was in the '18 time frame. You have a 87 cash margin profile that will be better than what it was in the '18 time frame largely driven by the -10 model mix.
finding: Boeing expected 737 cash margins to recover to 2018 levels by 2025-26 and 787 cash margins to exceed them because of the 787-10 mix.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: the cost of an airplane, 60% to 70% are parts. On the labor side, it's less than 15%, and that's touch labor, that's support labor and that's engineering resources.
finding: Boeing's airplane cost is dominated by purchased parts (60-70%), with labor under 15%, so supplier stability matters more to cost than union wages.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: last year, we had 1,576 net orders in our commercial business. We had over 600 in the fourth quarter alone. There's 5,600 airplanes in backlog in BCA
finding: Boeing booked 1,576 net commercial orders in 2023 for a 5,600-aircraft backlog, so its constraint was supply, not demand.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: we are the ones who made the decision to constrain rates on the 737 program below 38 per month until we feel like we're ready. And we'll feel the impact of that over the next several months.
finding: After the Alaska 1282 door-plug event Boeing self-imposed a 737 rate cap below 38/month, accepting near-term financial impact to stabilize quality.
trigger: Alaska Airlines Flight 1282 door plug blowout (Jan 5, 2024) and FAA audit
response: Self-imposed 737 production cap below 38/month

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: For years, we prioritized the movement of the airplane through the factory over getting it done right, and that's got to change.
finding: Boeing's CFO admits the company historically prioritized schedule flow over build quality and commits to reversing that priority.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: starting on March 1 of this year, we no longer travel work between Wichita and our fuselage supplier and Renton. It had been going on too long. So now we will only accept a fully conforming fuselage from Spirit, which means in the near term, there might be variability of supply.
finding: Boeing stopped accepting non-conforming Spirit fuselages, trading near-term supply variability for long-term predictability.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: Boeing more than 20 years ago probably got a little too far ahead of itself on the topic of outsourcing. And this is probably the example. We believe and Spirit believes that reintegrating these 2 companies is what's best for safety and for quality
finding: Boeing reversed its two-decade outsourcing strategy, pursuing reacquisition of Spirit AeroSystems on safety and quality grounds (contradicts earlier outsourcing posture).
trigger: Quality escapes at Spirit fuselage supply after Alaska 1282
response: Pursuing reintegration of Spirit AeroSystems

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: how important our investment-grade rating is to us. And we work very closely with the rating agencies. And I will say that if a transaction were to occur, we would not use equity, right? We would fund it with a mix of cash and debt.
finding: Boeing ranked its investment-grade rating highly and said a Spirit deal would be funded with cash and debt, not equity.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: we've got these 2 big shadow factories we discussed, one in the 787, one in the 737. We are intent on shutting them down as we exit this year and liquidating those -- that inventory
finding: Boeing planned to close its 737 and 787 rework shadow factories by end-2024 and deliver the inventoried aircraft.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: With regards to capital allocation and our framework, no change. We want to generate cash after having invested in our own growth and then delever the balance sheet. And as I've said, the investment grade rating is still a priority.
finding: Boeing's capital allocation order stayed invest in growth first, then delever, with investment-grade rating as a priority (persistence).

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: we believe the $10 billion of free cash flow that we put out there, it's going to take us longer to get there than we planned. It will be further out in that '25, '26 window.
finding: After Alaska 1282 Boeing pushed its $10B free cash flow target later in the 2025-26 window (change of position: delay).
response: Delayed $10B FCF target

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: in the quarter, our free cash flow will be a usage of somewhere between $4 billion and $4.5 billion, and that's higher than we originally planned back in January.
finding: Boeing guided Q1 2024 free cash outflow of $4-4.5B due to lower deliveries and working capital, worse than January plans.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: We are not at the moment where we can manage the near term for these financial outcomes because of the work at hand around stability.
finding: Boeing explicitly subordinated near-term financial outcomes to factory stability in early 2024.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: our objective is to keep with the practice that we had in the post-pandemic recovery, where we held the supply chain and pace them just ahead of final assembly.
finding: Boeing's supply-chain rule is to pace suppliers slightly ahead of final assembly rate, even during slowdowns.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: the first half the rates will be lower. Second half, they're going to be higher as we get towards that 38 per month. And beyond 38 per month will be up to the FAA.
finding: Boeing's 2024 737 plan targeted a return toward 38/month in H2, with any increase beyond 38 subject to FAA approval.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: On the anti-icing, that is an effort that we have swarmed our very best resources on to determine a design solution and we're making good progress on that front. That's likely going to take us until towards the end of the year.
finding: MAX 7/10 certification was gated by an engine anti-icing redesign expected to take until late 2024.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: first quarter, margins at BCA, because of the events of January 5 and everything I described, are going to be more like negative 20%.
finding: Boeing guided Q1 2024 BCA margins around -20% because of Alaska 1282 customer considerations and factory actions.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: those margins are going to get to historical levels in the '25, '26 timeframe because you're going to have shut down 2 shadow factories, you're going to have better mix going your way and you're going to have operating leverage from what we expect to be higher production rates.
finding: Boeing ties its return to historical BCA margins in 2025-26 to closing shadow factories, better mix and rate-driven operating leverage.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: rest assured that we have changed our underwriting standards in our defense business. We will not take on another fixed price development program.
finding: Boeing hardened its risk appetite by refusing further fixed-price development contracts after defense losses.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: there needs to be advanced engine technology and aerodynamic investment in order to get an airplane that's 20% to 30% more efficient than we are today. And that will not be rushed.
finding: Boeing sets a 20-30% efficiency gain, dependent on new engine and aero technology, as the bar for its next airplane and refuses to rush it.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: we're working on those capabilities, investing behind that innovation as we speak, and we'll continue to do that. And it's not going to be outside the envelope of the financials I described. But it is going to position us for the future. Whatever that future looks like, it's not the right moment.
finding: Boeing keeps next-platform work at the capability level, bounded by its financial framework, and says it is not the moment to launch.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: we spent $5 billion between R&D and CapEx in 2023. That was 20% plus higher than it was the previous year. So we are investing, and we're ready to do it. What it actually looks like? Too soon to say.
finding: Boeing raised combined R&D and capex to about $5B in 2023 (+20%) while keeping the product decision open.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: mistakes that matter are usually in the development of another airplane ... when you get big development programs wrong, you pay a price, and you pay it for a long time ... next leader has to be prepared to make smart long-term decisions and get the development programs right.
finding: Calhoun's parting advice was that new-airplane development is where big, lasting mistakes happen, which supports a cautious launch posture.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: working closely with the rating agencies, we believe we can do the move I described in the near term with market access without that.
finding: In April 2024 Boeing thought it could raise funds without issuing equity; it made a $24B capital raise in October 2024 (p.120).

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: We can move forward without full clarity. And as you probably know, we're not going to get involved in that, whatever is going on there. ... But we are not -- we're not being held hostage to that.
finding: Boeing pursued the Spirit deal without waiting for Airbus to settle how it would take back its own Spirit work.
trigger: Airbus negotiating to take back its work packages from Spirit AeroSystems
response: Proceed with Spirit acquisition without waiting for Airbus resolution; stay out of Airbus-Spirit talks

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: if we get to a moment where the buffers exceed that requirement, we will curtail but not until they exceed that requirement.
finding: Boeing keeps suppliers producing for the future 50-per-month rate and cuts orders only when buffers exceed that need.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: the FAA didn't demand that. We demanded it because it's -- we're determined to get ahead of it. ... And if we don't, we won't extend. We won't rate up. We won't do anything until it is under control
finding: Calhoun called the 2024 slowdown self-imposed and made rate increases depend on a controlled production system.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: The program booked about 300 basis points of impact in the quarter. And that was primarily driven by the delayed rate ramp that you're describing as well as mixing in more 8s and 9s for 10s in the near term
finding: The slower ramp and swapping -10s for -8s and -9s cut about 3 points off 737 program margin.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: If we get ourselves to 38, which is our first objective, and we do it in a steady fashion moving up another 12 in my view, is doable in the window that we're talking about. So that's the bet we're making
finding: Calhoun bet on reaching 50 737s per month by 2025-26; Ortberg later refused to set rate dates.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: there are a number of terms and issues we need to work through, including price, financing and other key items and the best approach to handling and potentially divesting certain work that Spirit does for other customers. ... we agreed to advance Spirit $425 million
finding: Boeing propped up Spirit with a $425M advance while negotiating to buy it and carve out its work for other customers.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: Longer term, we remain confident in our ability to achieve $10 billion of free cash flow. However ... we continue to expect that this goal will take us longer than we originally planned and later in the '25, '26 window, primarily tied to the 737 and 787 production delivery ramps of 50 per month and 10 per month
finding: Under Calhoun, Boeing kept the $10B free-cash-flow target for 2025-26 tied to 737 at 50 and 787 at 10; Ortberg later dropped the date.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: Revenue was $4.7 billion, and operating margin was minus 24.6%. These results were significantly lower than last year, primarily reflecting lower 737 deliveries and the 737-9 grounding impact for customer considerations of $443 million.
finding: The 737-9 grounding cost Boeing $443M in customer compensation, and commercial margins fell to -24.6%.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: As it pertains to the certification of the -7 and the -10, we coordinated with our customers and added more 8s and 9s into the skyline in the near term to mitigate impacts to their fleet needs and stabilize our production plans.
finding: When MAX 7/10 certification slipped, Boeing moved customers to certified -8s and -9s, a response Ortberg repeated in 2025.
response: Substitute 737-8/-9 deliveries in customer skylines

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: We're slowing near-term production and plan to return to 5 per month later this year. We expect to achieve rate increases, including 10 per month by 2026.
finding: In April 2024 Boeing targeted 10 787s per month by 2026, a goal it still held in late 2025.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: the product line holds up really well competitively. And we'll continue to compete campaign by campaign in this demand environment.
finding: Boeing says its product line is competitive and it fights for orders campaign by campaign.
trigger: Record 2023 orders industry-wide and customer frustration with Boeing delivery delays
response: Compete campaign by campaign; rely on product line strength

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: we do have flexibility in order for us, one, to be able to give them schedules that meet their fleet needs, albeit at reduced levels, but also confidence that in the future, we're going to get more predictable. ... We don't believe we need to make unnecessary trades.
finding: Boeing handled customers hurt by delivery delays by rescheduling within the backlog, not with broader trade-offs.
trigger: Customer frustration over 2024 production slowdown and late deliveries
response: Re-schedule backlog to meet fleet needs at reduced levels; avoid unnecessary trades

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: Now I also recognize that this can be disruptive, both operationally and financially. And we will, at times, frustrate both our customers and our shareholders. But this is the right time, and this is the right set of actions to take.
finding: Boeing accepted that its quality actions would frustrate customers and shareholders in the short term.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: We can't rush. We can't push the factory too hard or the system too hard because the payoff, if we do this right, is going to be big beyond 2025, and that's what we're aiming at.
finding: The 'don't rush the ramp' stance started under Calhoun and West in 2024, before Ortberg arrived.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: The CAAC has asked for additional validation on a lithium battery in that recorder. And because of that, we have not been delivering airplanes to China recently.
finding: Chinese regulatory actions repeatedly halted deliveries to China (2024 recorder battery, 2025 tariffs).

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: we expect the transaction to close mid-2025, subject to the satisfaction of customary closing conditions, including regulatory and Spirit shareholder approvals as well as the sale of Spirit operations related to certain Airbus commercial work packages.
finding: Boeing took its fuselage supply back in-house by buying Spirit, with Spirit's Airbus work packages split off to Airbus.
trigger: Spirit AeroSystems quality problems; shared supplier with Airbus
response: Acquire Spirit (~$4.7bn equity, $8.3bn EV)

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: We know that ASKs will be big. We know wage ASKs will be big. We're not afraid to treat our employees well in this process.
finding: Before the 2024 IAM talks Boeing said it would give sizeable wage increases to avoid a strike; members still rejected the offer and struck (p.156).

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: if we are able to bump up against maturities we're going to do what it takes to protect that rating, period. And we've been consistent since April 2020 on that front and evidenced by the Spirit financing decision.
finding: Protecting the investment-grade rating has been Boeing's fixed financial priority since 2020.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: what you saw in the quarter that we had a pullback of about $1 billion on the advance balance. Those two things are both happening in that balance
finding: Customers reacted to Boeing's delivery problems by applying excess advances and holding back pre-delivery payments, a $1B cash hit.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: the third line, it also helps us with unforeseen issues because it gives us flexibility across three lines as opposed to having to close two if we end up the nonconformance somewhere. So we are simply trying to overcapacitize to accommodate things that appear and steady our production.
finding: Boeing builds spare final-assembly capacity (a third Renton line) to absorb disruptions.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: On cash and marketable securities, we ended the quarter at $12.6 billion, reflecting the $10 billion issuance of new debt in May ... The debt balance increased to $57.9 billion driven by the new debt issuance.
finding: Boeing issued $10B of new debt in May 2024, taking debt to $57.9B.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: We'll continue to follow the lead of the FAA as we progress through the certification process and still expect first delivery in 2025.
finding: In July 2024 the 777X first delivery was still guided for 2025; it later moved to 2026 (October 2024) and 2027 (October 2025).

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: we announced a definitive agreement to acquire Spirit in an all-stock transaction worth approximately $4.7 billion with a total enterprise value of approximately $8.3 billion ... as well as the sale of Spirit operations related to certain Airbus commercial work packages.
finding: Boeing paid for Spirit in stock, and the deal required Spirit to sell its operations serving certain Airbus work packages.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: One of the most important actions we took was the transfer of our Renton fuselage inspection process to Wichita. On-site Boeing inspectors at Spirit increased by almost 3x the number that we had before January.
finding: Boeing moved fuselage inspection upstream to Spirit and tripled its inspectors there.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: we've identified an engineering solution for the engine anti-ice system for in-production aircraft that will be implemented and certified in 2025 to support the first delivery of our -7 and -10 in the MAX family.
finding: In July 2024 Boeing targeted 2025 certification of the 737-7/-10; it later slipped to 2026.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: Based on the lessons that we've learned in taking on these fixed-price development programs, we have maintained contracting discipline for all future opportunities.
finding: Calhoun had already sworn off risky fixed-price development bids, and Ortberg kept the stance.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: let me touch on the recently announced agreement to acquire Spirit AeroSystems. This is an important shift in strategic direction, and it would course correct the decision made decades ago.
finding: Calhoun called the Spirit AeroSystems buy-back a strategic shift that corrects Boeing's decades-old decision to outsource fuselage work.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: The January accident obviously sharpened this focus, leading us to take multiple additional steps to improve the stability of our operations, including major elements of our supply chain. First, among our actions was to slow things down and control traveled work, allowing our supply chain to catch up
finding: Boeing responded to the January 2024 accident by deliberately slowing 737 production and controlling traveled work so suppliers could catch up.
trigger: January 2024 Alaska Airlines 737-9 door plug accident and FAA 38/month cap
response: Deliberately slow production, control traveled work, build supply-chain buffer

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: So we are perfectly comfortable to supplement our liquidity position to support these two objectives. And we're constantly evaluating our capital structure and liquidity levels to ensure that we could satisfy our debt maturities over the next 18 months while keeping confidence in our credit rating as investment grade.
finding: In September 2024 Boeing said it was ready to raise capital to protect its rating; it announced a $24B raise in October (p.120).
lag: about 1 month before the October 2024 capital raise

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: on the 37 cash margins, when we get to a point where we're more stable and hitting the rates you described, we are going to be approaching what those cash margins look like in the 2018 time frame. On the 787 program, similarly, as we move forward towards those rates we've described, we're going to be better than 2018.
finding: Boeing expects 737 unit cash margins to return to 2018 levels and 787 margins to beat them at target rates (50+ and 10).

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: On the 777, we expect lower deliveries than last year, driven to a large extent by engine availability. That has been a constraint.
finding: Engine availability limited 777 deliveries in 2024.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: 787, there will be no change in the part supply chain expectations, right? That's just going to keep going. If there's a non-787 part that is behind, we're going to allow suppliers to catch up. If there are non-787 parts that are not behind and there's a safety stock, they are going to stop.
finding: Boeing's strike rule for suppliers: keep 787 parts flowing, let late suppliers catch up, and stop suppliers that are ahead.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: From a financial perspective, any impact is going to be dictated by the duration of the work stoppage ... strike will impact production and deliveries and operations and will jeopardize our recovery. So our immediate focus is to the laser-like focused on actions to conserve cash, and we will.
finding: The day after the IAM contract was rejected, Boeing switched to cash conservation.
trigger: IAM members rejected the tentative contract (96%) and began striking (Sep 2024)
response: Immediate cash-conservation actions; CEO on factory floor to reset union relationship

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: An example, just the 767 freighter. We looked at that and said, "Hey, look, there's an incoming on the 767 freighter. It's coming soon. Let's make the decision now and get that distraction out of the way.
finding: Boeing ended 767 Freighter production ahead of an approaching ('incoming') deadline to free resources.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: I don't think we can walk away from these contracts. These are our core customers that need this capability. ... So walking away isn't an answer to this.
finding: Boeing will not cancel loss-making core contracts outright and renegotiates them instead.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: It is so much more important that we do this right than fast coming out of the chute. ... We've tried to manage that as best we could and keep folks like Spirit, for example, on fuselage, keep them funded and moving forward.
finding: Boeing kept funding critical suppliers such as Spirit through the strike and chose a slow restart.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: This is not a situation where we have to figure out what market opportunities are we going to go pursue. They're right in front of us. Our backlog is so strong.
finding: Ortberg ranks executing the existing backlog above pursuing new market opportunities.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: So we're going to really focus this workforce reduction in streamlining those overhead activities ... And I wouldn't think of it like we're going to take people off the production or out of the engineering labs.
finding: Boeing's layoffs targeted overhead and spared production and engineering staff.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: Yes, it's too early for me to answer that. I would just say all the financial forecast, the long-term outlook are under review.
finding: In October 2024 Ortberg would not back the $10B free-cash-flow target; by mid-2025 he called it a question of when, not if.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: I think that we're better off being -- doing less and doing it better than doing more and not doing it well.
finding: Ortberg prefers a narrower portfolio executed well to a broad one.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: We're focused on maintaining $10 billion of cash in addition to our revolver capacity as we historically have.
finding: Boeing keeps a minimum cash balance of about $10B plus its revolver.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: we have a plan to comprehensively address the balance sheet in the near term that could include an offering of equity and equity-linked securities.
finding: Boeing planned to repair its balance sheet with equity and equity-linked securities.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: we ended the quarter at $10.5 billion, primarily reflecting the $2 billion use of free cash flow in the quarter. The debt balance remained stable, ending at $57.7 billion. Last week, we entered into a new $10 billion short-term credit facility
finding: Boeing's liquidity fell to $10.5B against $57.7B of debt, and it added a new $10B short-term credit line.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: We've worked across our supply chain partners to significantly reduce expenditures while balancing the associated trade-offs. We shared plans to reduce our workforce to align with our financial reality and a more focused set of priorities. We're decisively implementing reductions to our discretionary spending across the company.
finding: In a liquidity crisis Boeing cut supplier spend, headcount and discretionary costs.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: Revenue was $7.4 billion, and operating margin was minus 54%, primarily reflecting previously announced pre-tax charges of $3 billion on the 777X and 767 programs
finding: The strike and program charges drove commercial margins to -54% in Q3 2024.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: Given the strike and our need to conserve cash, we've made near-term adjustments to broadly stop supplier shipments. We continue to manage supplier by supplier based on inventory levels and for certain suppliers, this will allow them to catch up.
finding: During the 2024 IAM strike Boeing stopped most supplier shipments to save cash, managing each supplier separately.
trigger: September 2024 IAM machinist strike halting Puget Sound production
response: Broadly stop supplier shipments; manage supplier by supplier; keep critical suppliers funded

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: the $2.6 billion pretax charge primarily reflects our latest assessment of the certification time lines to address the delays in flight testing of the 777-9 as well as anticipated delays associated with the IAM work stoppage. ... now expect first delivery in 2026.
finding: The 777X slipped to 2026 with a $2.6B charge in 2024, the first of the Ortberg-era 777X resets (another followed in October 2025).

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: This include disciplined program and risk management in all phases of the project, including the bid phase.
finding: Boeing applies risk discipline from the bid phase of new programs.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: Boeing's an airplane company. And at the right time in the future, we need to develop a new airplane but we have a lot of work to do before them. This includes stabilizing our business, improving the execution on the development programs, streamlining the portfolio to do what we do well and restoring the balance sheet
finding: From his first call Ortberg made a new airplane conditional on stabilisation, finished development programs, a streamlined portfolio and a restored balance sheet, and he held this position through 2025.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: First, we need a fundamental culture change in the company; second, we must stabilize the business; third, we need to improve our execution discipline on new platform commitments across the company; and fourth, while doing the first 3, we must build a new future for Boeing.
finding: Ortberg's 4-point plan puts culture, stabilisation and execution ahead of building the future (new products).

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: we've got a backlog that is in place that has embedded escalation in it. That hasn't changed. That's good. And in terms of our supply contracts, they're vastly signed up until end of this decade.
finding: Escalation clauses in the backlog and supplier contracts locked to 2030 protect commercial margins from inflation.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: we've got $87.5 billion worth of inventory in the company right now. That is too much. Now it's been an investment and stability
finding: Boeing held $87.5B of inventory, a deliberate stability buffer it expects to turn into cash.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: I'm not putting a finer point on it, both externally nor internally. We're going to go to that rate when the KPIs say that we're going to go to that rate.
finding: Ortberg sets no rate-increase dates, even internally; KPIs decide the timing.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: they've got a big challenge with supporting our rate increases, our competitor rate increases and managing the aftermarket. And I work very closely with Larry and his team to make sure we stay aligned.
finding: Boeing competes with Airbus's ramps and the aftermarket for GE/CFM engine supply and manages this at CEO level.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: the IAM agreement did put pressure. But keep in mind, we're talking about a cost that's less than 5% of the airplane.
finding: Boeing says the IAM wage settlement adds pressure but amounts to under 5% of airplane cost.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: it's an important technology development program. It's very challenging. ... And then we'll look at what comes out of that and how that factors into our next airplane. ... We've got some funding we're investing, but we've also got some funding there to support us.
finding: Boeing co-funds the X-66 NASA technology demonstrator as an input to its next airplane, sharing the cost of pre-launch R&D.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: because we've forecasted rates that the supply chain has built to and then we haven't met those rates. So I want to make sure that supply chain isn't making independent decisions on readiness for these out-year production rates and continuing to invest in the capacity that they need to supply us.
finding: Boeing admits suppliers lost faith after it missed forecast rates and is working to keep them investing in capacity.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: it's generally more in the commodities where there's long lead components like forgings, castings, that kind of stuff. I'm less worried about electronics. ... it's where you have to invest in that second and third tier supply chain that we want to make sure that they're making those investments and they haven't hedged their bets.
finding: Long-lead forgings and castings at lower supplier tiers are the rate-limiting part of the supply chain.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
